Below are two statements and a set of excerpts from one author's body of writing (the corpus). For each statement, answer only YES or NO: does the corpus agree with this statement? No third answer is permitted: not "partly", "mostly" or "it depends". After the word, give one line naming the excerpt numbers your answer rests on, or "none".

Output plain text only, exactly:
S-001<TAB>YES or NO<TAB>excerpts: ...
S-002<TAB>YES or NO<TAB>excerpts: ...

The statements:
S-001: Happy families are all alike.
S-002: Every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.

The corpus excerpts (retrieved mechanically by term match; line numbers refer to the corpus file):

War and Peace explores numerous themes. One of the most prominent is the interplay between individual lives and the sweep of history. Tolstoy illustrates how personal happiness and tragedy are deeply entwined with national events. Characters make choices that shape their destinies, but they are also subject to forces beyond their control. The novel examines the nature of war, portraying it as chaotic, brutal, and devoid of the glory often assigned to it in patriotic narratives. It criticises the romanticised views of war and emphasises the suffering of soldiers and civilians alike. Love and family are also central. Romantic love, such as that between Andrei and Natasha, is portrayed as both beautiful and fragile, easily shattered by pride and betrayal. Family bonds provide comfort and meaning, but they can also be a source of obligation and sacrifice. Tolstoy also delves into themes of faith and spiritual searching. Pierres journey through Freemasonry and encounters with simple people like Platon Karataev reflect Tolstoys interest in authentic spirituality versus institutional religion. The novel debates free will versus determinism: do people shape events, or are they swept along by a tide of history? Tolstoy leans toward a view that individuals have moral agency in small matters but are constrained by broader historical forces. Another theme is the illusion of control. Characters like Napoleon and Andrei aspire to master their destinies, but they are humbled by circumstances they cannot predict. Finally, the novel contemplates the meaning of peace, suggesting that peace is not merely the absence of war but a state of harmony achieved through love, humility, and a recognition of human limitations.

It wasn’t like that in our day. The more deeply I fell in love, the more disembodied she became for me. Returning from there I married. The new conditions of happy family life completely diverted me from all search for the general meaning of life. My whole life was centred at that time in my family, wife and children, and therefore in care to increase our means of livelihood. My striving after self-perfection, for which I had already substituted a striving for perfection in general, i.e. progress, was now again replaced by the effort simply to secure the best possible conditions for myself and my family.

He knows that it has not worked out too well, but when he starts to consider the reasons for this he cannot blame himself for having got things seriously wrong. ‘How can that be when I did everything properly?’ It is true that at the very end Ivan Ilyich appears to grasp Tolstoy’s truth that a life lived wrongly is an obstacle to an easy death. He does conclude that his only real happiness was in childhood and just afterwards, and that there was something disgustingly unsatisfactory about the second half of his life. Finally he sees the light, and is permitted to die. But the purity of this vision of an unhappy adulthood is subject to some doubt. Is this not a fairly common experience, even without the promptings of severe illness? Did not the author himself see his life as pointless at precisely the same age (Ivan is also forty-one)? And, in any case, is he not suffering from blurred perceptions because of the pain he has suffered and the opium he is now being treated with? This is to say that there is something amiss with Tolstoy’s moral purpose here. But there is one thing we can be reasonably sure of: if a miracle had occurred and he had survived, Ivan Ilyich would probably not have gone on to live his life differently, soulfully, newly inspired by his close encounter with death. He would have been more likely to return to his fractious family life and his cards. The life of this man has been trivial rather than despicable, and it is unfair of the author to adopt such a disparaging attitude towards his protagonist. To accept Tolstoy’s implied disparagement would be to condemn and dismiss the lives of millions of people carrying on as best they can in a difficult world without doing much harm to others. The idea implicit in this story that we should emerge from reading it determined to reshape our misguided lives is rather unrealistic. #### **THE DEATH OF IVAN ILYICH**

2.5 — The Moral Ramifications of Concealment: The Lie as Load Transfer Definition: A lie is not primarily false speech. A lie is the selfish act of obtaining closure without paying principal. It protects one mind from the felt pressure of obligation while transferring the compounding structural load onto others. Concealment is therefore not neutral comfort. It is debt outsourcing. Mechanism: Ledger Gravity cannot be erased by comfort (See: 1.6). The Wall can only reroute it. When an agent lies or cooperates with anesthetic, they reduce their own awareness and therefore their felt suffering. But the debt remains in the structure, so it expresses elsewhere: in family systems, co-workers, institutions, and future timelines. This is why the King in Yellow's technique begins with the whisper of uniqueness (See: 4.1, 3.3.1): it justifies private deferral. Ledger Consequence: Principal remains unpaid. Interest is externalized. The liar pays less now and invoices the collective later. This is profound moral cowardice, not because it is socially impolite, but because it is structurally predatory: it increases total suffering while simulating relief. The endgame of accumulated load transfer is Carcosa (See: 3.3): a closure state where the system collapses into rerun because truth has become too expensive. Phenomenology: Lying feels like immediate relief. It often feels like 'keeping the peace.' Downstream, it feels like inexplicable conflict in unrelated areas: children acting out, friendships decaying, systems failing for no visible reason. These are the displaced payments. Narrative Function: This framework converts the epic's ethics into physics. The villainy of the Anesthetic System is not sin; it is accounting fraud. Andrei, recovering from his wound at Bald Hills, returns home disillusioned. His wife Lise dies in childbirth while he is away, leaving him with a son but plunging him into despair. He withdraws from society and from military service, preferring to live quietly with his father and sister. He becomes critical of the world around him, seeing it as a web of vanity and deception. These events illustrate Tolstoy's central theme that the search for glory, wealth, or social approval cannot satisfy the deeper needs of the soul. War strips away delusions; personal tragedies reveal the fragility of happiness; and the characters begin to wrestle with questions of fate, duty, and the meaning of life. Tolstoy also introduces the character of Dolokhov more fully in these chapters. Dolokhov is a daring officer known for his reckless courage and cunning. After the duel, he continues to cross paths with the Rostovs and Pierre, showing different facets of his personality: he flirts with Sonya, loses his fortune at cards, and later demonstrates bravery and loyalty on the battlefield. The interplay of characters like Dolokhov and Denisov (Nicholas's good-natured commander) underscores the variety of responses individuals have to war and social pressures. By juxtaposing the exhilaration and horror of battle with the petty intrigues of Petersburg society and the warmth of domestic life in Moscow, Tolstoy portrays the complexity of Russian society during this era. He emphasises that history is not driven by great men alone but by a multitude of individuals making choices under circumstances they cannot control. As Pierre, Andrei, and Nicholas navigate these shifting landscapes, they embody different responses to the chaos of war and the emptiness of social convention. Andrei's disillusionment, Pierre's spiritual quest, and Nicholas's naive patriotism foreshadow their future growth and suffering as the conflict with Napoleon intensifies. The war is both an external force that disrupts lives and an internal catalyst that forces characters to confront their beliefs and desires.

And he was the only one who knew it; the people around him didn’t know, or didn’t want to know - they thought that everything in the world was going on as before. This was what tormented Ivan Ilyich more than anything. He could see that his family - especially his wife and daughter, whose visiting season was in full swing - had no inkling; it annoyed them that he was not much fun and asked so much of them - as if he was to blame. Despite their best efforts to hide it, he could see that he was in their way. His wife had developed an attitude to his illness and she was sticking to it whatever he might say or do. Her attitude went like this: ‘You know what it’s like,’ she would say to her friends. ‘Ivan Ilyich can’t be like other people. He won’t stick to his treatment. One moment he takes his drops and eats what he’s supposed to, and goes to bed when he should; the next day, if I’m not watching him, he doesn’t take his medicine, he eats sturgeon which he’s not allowed - and he stays up playing whist until one in the morning.’ ‘Oh, come on,’ says Ivan Ilyich. ‘I did that once, with Pyotr Ivanovich.’ ‘What about yesterday, with Shebek?’ ‘It made no difference. I couldn’t sleep with all that pain ...’ ‘Well, it doesn’t matter why. Only you’ll never get better like that, and it’s getting us down.’ Praskovya’s attitude towards Ivan Ilyich’s illness, of which she made no secret to other people or to him, was that it was all his fault; he was making his wife’s life a misery yet again. Ivan Ilyich felt she was doing this unconsciously, but that didn’t make things any easier for him. In court Ivan Ilyich noticed, or thought he noticed, the same strange attitude towards him. There were times when he thought people were watching him closely like a man who was about to give up his job; at other times his associates would make friendly little jokes about the way he worried over his health, as if this ghastly, fearful, unheard-of thing that had got going inside him and was now incessantly gnawing at him and inexorably taking him away was a good subject and a laughing matter. The one who infuriated him most was Schwartz, with his playfulness, *joie de* *vivre* and all-round respectability which recalled the Ivan Ilyich of ten years before.
